cells.C4: Start with gratitude for your body and the life it has enabled you to live.
cells.D4:
Cherish your body; it is yours for this one time only.

Jack Kornfield, After the Ecstasy, the Laundry
cells.E4: Place a hand on your heart and silently thank your body for carrying you this far.
cells.F4: Write a short thank-you letter to your body, naming three moments it showed strength.
cells.G4: Look at yourself in the mirror and say one kind thing about a part of your body.
cells.H4: Create a small ritual after showers to oil your skin and honor its resilience.
cells.I4: Reflect on 3 major life events and how your body supported you through them.
cells.J4: Draw a timeline of your body's journey: injuries, achievements, changes, and what each taught you.
cells.C5: Deep, regular sleep helps protect memory, immune health, and mood. Create a calming pre-sleep ritual and aim for 7 to 8 hours each night.
cells.D5:
Just like exercise, sleep is its own kind of wonder drug.

Peter Attia, Outlive
cells.E5: Dim the lights or light a candle an hour before bed and let the day soften.
cells.F5: Make a bedtime playlist that calms you deeply and use it all week.
cells.G5: Put your phone away 30 mins before bed tonight.
cells.H5: Design a full wind-down routine: warm bath, herbal tea, no screens, 10pm sleep.
cells.I5: Read about sleep cycles and the link between aging and deep sleep.
cells.J5: Track your sleep for 14 days and analyze your patterns.
cells.C6: Lean toward whole foods linked to slower cellular aging: leafy greens, berries, olive oil, nuts. Drink plenty of water.
cells.D6:
The best approximation for an anti-wrinkle diet is one that's centered around whole plant foods.

Michael Greger, How Not to Age
cells.E6: Sip a warm herbal tea slowly, feeling it nourish you.
cells.F6: Before each meal today, pause for a small thank-you.
cells.G6: Eat a handful of nuts or berries instead of chips today.
cells.H6: Plan a week of whole-food meals built around seasonal vegetables.
cells.I6: Read about how Mediterranean diets slow cognitive decline.
cells.J6: Study Blue Zones' dietary habits and create a food journal to apply them.
cells.C7: Walk, stretch, or dance each day, not to fix your body, but to enjoy living in it.
cells.D7:
Embrace the reality that movement is as important as brushing your teeth.

Gabrielle Lyon, Forever Strong
cells.E7: Put on your favorite song and sway gently for 2 minutes.
cells.F7: Dance alone for 10 minutes to music that lifts your spirit.
cells.G7: Do 5 minutes of gentle stretching this morning.
cells.H7: Take a dance, yoga, or movement class just for fun, not fitness.
cells.I7: Remember a way of moving you loved as a child. Could it come back?
cells.J7: After a week of joyful movement, write down how your mood and energy have shifted.
cells.C8: Replace ‘getting old’ with ‘growing wise’. Seeing aging as a time of expansion, not decline, lifts your well-being.
cells.D8:
Even if we are the product of the past, we are still the architects of our future.

Matthieu Ricard, Beyond the Self
cells.E8: Say out loud: “I'm growing wiser, not older.” Notice how it feels.
cells.F8: Collect 3 quotes that celebrate aging and place them where you'll see them.
cells.G8: Replace the word “old” with “wise” in your self-talk for one day.
cells.H8: Make a vision board showing what you want from the next decade.
cells.I8: List myths about aging and contrast them with research-backed truths.
cells.J8: Write a page about how you'd like to see your own aging from now on.
cells.C9: Clear physical and mental clutter to reduce stress. Let go of what no longer serves you, from outdated beliefs to unused possessions.
cells.D9:
We don't need to believe everything our thoughts tell us.

Elizabeth Blackburn, The Telomere Effect
cells.E9: Close your eyes for 2 minutes and let go of one old belief with each out-breath.
cells.F9: Picture your worries as clouds and watch them drift away.
cells.G9: Clear one drawer or surface you use daily.
cells.H9: Declutter one small area each day for a week, at home or in your calendar.
cells.I9: Make a list of beliefs you've outgrown and why.
cells.J9: Draw a mind map of what fills your head; choose three things to let go of on purpose.
cells.C10: Add two short strength sessions this week: bodyweight, bands, or weights all count. Strength isn't about how you look: it's what keeps you independent as you age.
cells.D10:
The currency of healthy aging is muscle—lean, high-performance muscle.

Mark Hyman, Young Forever
cells.E10: Next time you stand up from a chair, notice the strength in your legs.
cells.F10: Do a set of squats and feel the quiet pride of muscles at work.
cells.G10: Do 10 bodyweight squats or wall push-ups right now.
cells.H10: Start a twice-weekly strength routine: squats, push-ups, rows, and a plank.
cells.I10: Think of one daily task that would get easier if you were stronger.
cells.J10: Look up strength guidelines for your age and sketch a 4-week plan.
cells.C11: Practice noticing your emotions without being ruled by them. This flexibility supports your mental health and gentler relationships.
cells.D11:
The aim is not to cease to experience emotions but to avoid being enslaved by them.

Matthieu Ricard, Beyond the Self
cells.E11: Name what you're feeling right now, without judging it.
cells.F11: Track your emotions daily for a week to notice patterns.
cells.G11: Take 3 deep breaths when upset before reacting.
cells.H11: Try the RAIN method (Recognize, Allow, Investigate, Nurture) during a strong emotion.
cells.I11: Write about a recent emotional reaction: where might it have come from?
cells.J11: Study Susan David's work and apply her “show up, step out, walk your why” process.
cells.C12: Talk to yourself as you would to a friend. Be gentle with your inner critic: a harsh inner voice can weigh on you more than the years.
cells.D12:
The point is not to perfect yourself. It is to perfect your love.

Jack Kornfield, No Time Like the Present
cells.E12: When you make a mistake, whisper: “It's okay, you're doing your best.”
cells.F12: Write a letter from your inner critic, then answer it with kindness.
cells.G12: Place a hand on your heart whenever a self-critical thought arises.
cells.H12: Listen to a self-compassion meditation before bed every night for a week.
cells.I12: Write down one harsh thing you often tell yourself, then rewrite it gently.
cells.J12: Take Kristin Neff's free self-compassion test and reflect on your results.
cells.C13: Watch something funny, recall a ridiculous memory, or laugh with a friend. Lightness is medicine.
cells.D13:
Add humor, hugs, and laughter.

Linda Bacon, Body Respect
cells.E13: Watch a short funny animal video. Let yourself giggle.
cells.F13: Share an embarrassing memory with a trusted friend and laugh together.
cells.G13: Make a silly face at yourself in the mirror.
cells.H13: Attend a live comedy night or improv class.
cells.I13: Remember a time humor helped you through something hard.
cells.J13: Keep a funny journal for a week: one laugh a day.
cells.C14: Notice resistance to change. Practice softening around it. Acceptance isn't resignation: it's clarity.
cells.D14:
Hell is resistance. Heaven is acceptance.

Stephen Levine, Who Dies?
cells.E14: When discomfort comes, say softly: “This too belongs.”
cells.F14: Sit for 5 minutes with an uncomfortable truth, without trying to fix it.
cells.G14: Write down what you're resisting today, then tear up the paper.
cells.H14: For 3 days, notice and name each moment of resistance, without acting on it.
cells.I14: What is the difference between giving up and accepting?
cells.J14: Write a short dialogue between the part of you that resists and the part that accepts.
cells.C15: Journal, pray, chant, or sit in nature. Caring for your soul deepens resilience and joy as you age.
cells.D15:
Life purpose is what brings us eudaemonic happiness, the healthy feeling that we are involved in something bigger than ourselves.

Elizabeth Blackburn, The Telomere Effect
cells.E15: Sit under a tree for 5 minutes, doing nothing.
cells.F15: Pray, chant or sit in silence for 10 minutes each morning for a week.
cells.G15: Light a candle and write down 3 thoughts from your soul.
cells.H15: Build a mini sacred space in your room with items that calm you.
cells.I15: What does “soul” mean to you, and when do you feel close to it?
cells.J15: Start a soul journal: each evening, one moment that felt meaningful.
cells.C16: Choose one small part of your day to improve: how you eat, move, rest, or connect. Small shifts, big ripples.
cells.D16:
There is always a step small enough from where we are to get us to where we want to be.

Ellen Langer, Counterclockwise
cells.E16: Notice when in the day you feel most alive.
cells.F16: Track your daily highs and lows for one week and adjust your routine.
cells.G16: Shift one habit: walk after lunch or eat dinner earlier.
cells.H16: Draw your ideal day, balancing energy, rest and connection, and live it for 3 days.
cells.I16: When does your energy dip today? What came just before?
cells.J16: Study circadian rhythms and optimize your schedule accordingly.
cells.C17: Reach out and let yourself be vulnerable. Share a story. Be seen and heard. Aging well includes loving well.
cells.D17:
Evidently, a loving brain lives a happier and longer life.

Lisa Mosconi, Brain Food
cells.E17: Text someone: “Thinking of you. Grateful you're in my life.”
cells.F17: Share a recent struggle with someone you feel safe with.
cells.G17: Schedule a 10-min call with a friend you haven't talked to in a while.
cells.H17: Initiate a monthly “truth dinner” with a friend: phones off, deep talk.
cells.I17: With whom do you hold back, and why?
cells.J17: Read Brené Brown's work and outline what real connection means for you.
cells.C18: Take 10 to 15 minutes to simply sit and observe your breath, thoughts, and feelings without judgment. Eat one mindful meal today without distractions.
cells.D18:
The present moment is filled with joy and happiness. If you are attentive, you will see it.

Thich Nhat Hanh, Peace Is Every Step
cells.E18: Eat one grape slowly and attentively, noticing every detail.
cells.F18: Walk in silence for 15 minutes, noticing sensations and thoughts.
cells.G18: Set a 5-minute timer and simply follow your breath.
cells.H18: Take a full mindful meal: no phone, no conversation, just you and the food.
cells.I18: Read Thich Nhat Hanh's “How to Eat” or “The Miracle of Mindfulness.”
cells.J18: Keep a presence log for a week: what brought you into the now, what pulled you away.
cells.C19: Write, paint, play, or dance. Creative play is food for the soul and mind.
cells.D19:
Pen your poem, dance your dance, express the depths of your own heart.

Jack Kornfield, No Time Like the Present
cells.E19: Doodle freely for 5 minutes, without judging.
cells.F19: Spend 30 minutes on a creative project you've long ignored.
cells.G19: Write one haiku about your day.
cells.H19: Sign up for a creative workshop: painting, photography, pottery.
cells.I19: How has your creativity changed over the years?
cells.J19: Plan 30 days of small creative acts, one a day.
cells.C20: Mentor, volunteer, or simply tell stories. Your legacy takes shape in how you show up, starting today.
cells.D20:
I'm holding on to my torch. I'll let other people light theirs from mine.

Daniel Levitin, Successful Aging
cells.E20: Tell a story from your past to someone younger.
cells.F20: Write a letter of advice to your 25-year-old self and share it.
cells.G20: Offer a helpful tip to someone facing something you've been through.
cells.H20: Start mentoring someone in your field or life path.
cells.I20: List the key lessons life has taught you.
cells.J20: Build a “wisdom map” of lessons, stories and images you'd like to pass on.
cells.C21: Curiosity is youthfulness in disguise. Try or learn one new thing today: a language, an instrument, a skill. Your brain keeps its power to learn far longer than we think.
cells.D21:
You are never too old to set another goal or to dream a new dream.

L. Brown in Mark Hyman, Young Forever
cells.E21: Read 2 pages from a new book or article.
cells.F21: Join a local language, dance, or pottery class.
cells.G21: Try a new recipe or game this week.
cells.H21: Set a goal to learn one new thing a month and track it.
cells.I21: Research the brain's ability to learn later in life.
cells.J21: Design a 3-month learning plan around a passion you've ignored.
cells.C22: Identify one grudge or resentment you're holding. Take a first step toward forgiveness, not for the other person, but for your own freedom and peace.
cells.D22:
Every day I make mistakes, and every day I try to forgive myself for them.

Peter Attia, Outlive
cells.E22: Say softly: “I am willing to forgive.” Notice any tension.
cells.F22: Write a letter to someone you haven't forgiven (no need to send it).
cells.G22: Take a deep breath each time bitterness rises.
cells.H22: Try the Ho'oponopono forgiveness mantra daily for 2 weeks.
cells.I22: How has holding on affected your peace of mind?
cells.J22: Read about the science of forgiveness and how it affects health and aging.
cells.C23: Spend 20 minutes outdoors mindfully: walk in a park, sit by water, or garden. Time in nature reduces stress and supports well-being.
cells.D23:
Don't hold yourself captive; get out there and bathe in nature!

Max Lugavere, The Genius Life
cells.E23: Sit by an open window or on your balcony and feel the breeze.
cells.F23: Take a mindful walk barefoot in the grass or on a forest path.
cells.G23: Water a plant slowly, feeling each motion.
cells.H23: Plan a weekend day in nature: hike, picnic, or silent forest walk.
cells.I23: Recall a place in nature where you felt at peace. What made it so?
cells.J23: After each time outdoors this week, write a few lines about how you feel.
cells.C24: Some things about growing older can only be met with grace: less speed, less energy, less certainty. The aging body, the slower pace. This is memento mori.
cells.D24:
We need to learn to see our physical form as a river. Our body is not a static thing—it changes all the time.

Thich Nhat Hanh, You Are Here
cells.E24: Sit quietly for 2 minutes and say: “I am allowed to slow down.” Notice what softens.
cells.F24: Write a thank-you and farewell to something your younger body could do.
cells.G24: Do one everyday task today at half your usual speed, on purpose.
cells.H24: Adjust one routine to fit your energy now (a shorter walk, an earlier night) and keep it for a week.
cells.I24: Reflect on one limit that has brought you an unexpected gift.
cells.J24: Read about memento mori or impermanence and write what a good old age means to you.

cells.C4: Spend today simply observing your digital habits without judgment. What do you reach for? When and why?
cells.D4:
Principle #1: Clutter is costly.

Cal Newport, Digital Minimalism
cells.E4: After scrolling, notice: do you feel energized or drained? Name one feeling.
cells.F4: For one day, notice how you feel just before and just after each time you pick up your phone.
cells.G4: For one hour, count your phone pickups. Just count, no judgment.
cells.H4: Each evening for a week, check your screen-time report and note your top 3 apps.
cells.I4: What made you reach for your phone today: boredom, stress, habit? Write the first answer that comes.
cells.J4: For 3 evenings, journal about one pickup: what were you feeling just before?
cells.C5: Get clear on your reasons for doing this detox. Before opening any app today, ask: ‘What am I seeking?’ and ‘When will I know I'm done?’
cells.D5:
This is your life—what do you want to pay attention to?

Catherine Price, How to Break Up with Your Phone
cells.E5: Hold your phone for a moment before unlocking it. Feel the pull, then decide.
cells.F5: Each morning this week, close your eyes and picture a calmer day with less screen time. How does it feel?
cells.G5: Before opening an app, pause and say out loud what you hope to get from it.
cells.H5: Record a short voice note on why you're doing this detox. Replay it when your motivation dips.
cells.I5: Write down your top 3 reasons for this detox. Circle the one that matters most.
cells.J5: Write one clear goal, for example: ‘I'll cut screen time by 2 hours a day to make room for hobbies.’ Review it every Sunday.
cells.C6: List your most-used apps, sites and platforms. For each, ask: does this nourish me or drain me?
cells.D6:
When you pay attention to something you don’t especially value, it’s not an exaggeration to say that you’re paying with your life.

Oliver Burkeman, Four Thousand Weeks
cells.E6: Notice which apps leave you tense and which leave you calm. Name the feeling.
cells.F6: For 3 days, rate each app from −5 (draining) to +5 (nourishing) by how you feel after using it.
cells.G6: List your top 5 apps and delete one you don't really need.
cells.H6: Move every draining app off your home screen into one folder, and leave it there for a week.
cells.I6: Ask of your most-used app: would I download it again today? Write your answer and why.
cells.J6: Over a week, journal about the platform you use most: what does it give you, and what does it cost you?
cells.C7: Silence non-essential notifications, especially social media, shopping and news.
cells.D7:
The art of being wise is the art of knowing what to overlook.

W. James in Oliver Burkeman, Meditations for Mortals
cells.E7: Turn off one non-essential alert and notice how you feel: relief, or a little anxiety?
cells.F7: Keep your phone on silent for 3 days. Each evening, notice how calm or restless you felt.
cells.G7: Turn off lock-screen previews, so messages wait until you choose to look.
cells.H7: Turn on Do Not Disturb for one full afternoon and notice what you get done.
cells.I7: Which notification pulls you away most often? Write down what it really needs from you.
cells.J7: For a week, jot down each alert that interrupted something important. Then decide which ones deserve to stay.
cells.C8: Unfollow accounts that trigger comparison or anxiety. Follow only what uplifts or teaches you.
cells.D8:
Your smartphone is mostly just other people’s agenda for you.

Emma Seppälä, Sovereign
cells.E8: Scroll your feed for one minute and notice where jealousy or irritation shows up in your body.
cells.F8: For a week, notice how each app leaves you feeling, and follow five accounts that bring you calm or creativity.
cells.G8: Spend 10 minutes unfollowing accounts on Instagram or YouTube that no longer serve you.
cells.H8: Hide your main feed for a week with a feed blocker, and visit only the accounts you choose.
cells.I8: Which content fits your values, and which doesn't? Write one line for each.
cells.J8: Write your own short content rule: what earns a place in your feed, and why?
cells.C9: Designate at least one space in your home (like the dining table or bedroom) as tech-free. Move your charging spot outside your bedroom to discourage late-night scrolling and morning phone checks.
cells.D9:
Fill the center of your life... with things that reward creativity, relationship, and engagement.

Andy Crouch, The Tech-Wise Family
cells.E9: Sit in bed without your phone one night and notice how it feels.
cells.F9: Keep your phone out of the bedroom for a week and note changes in your sleep and mood.
cells.G9: Move your charger from your nightstand to the hallway.
cells.H9: Make a visible tech-free sign or basket for your dining table.
cells.I9: List the spaces at home that could use screen-free rules.
cells.J9: Write your own house rule: ‘No screens in [room], because it's a space for…’
cells.C10: Before checking social media, write down 3 things you're grateful for in your real life.
cells.D10:
Reconnect with a part of you that knows that life doesn’t happen on a screen.

Catherine Price, How to Break Up with Your Phone
cells.E10: Name one thing you're grateful for before you open social media.
cells.F10: For a week, pause before each scroll and savor one good moment from your day for 30 seconds.
cells.G10: Write one thing you're grateful for on a sticky note and put it on your phone.
cells.H10: For a week, write 3 good things in a notebook before your first scroll of the day.
cells.I10: Does comparing yourself online dim your gratitude? Write about one recent moment.
cells.J10: For 7 days, log your gratitude and your screen time side by side. What do you notice?
cells.C11: Craft a screen-free morning ritual: meditation, stretching, journaling, or just slow tea.
cells.D11:
When we know what to say no to, we can say yes to the things that matter.

Ryan Holiday, Stillness Is the Key
cells.E11: Start one day with 5 minutes of silence or tea before looking at your phone.
cells.F11: For a week, notice how your mood feels on mornings you don't check your phone first.
cells.G11: Use a real alarm clock and leave your phone in another room overnight.
cells.H11: Plan a simple 3-step morning routine and follow it for 3 days.
cells.I11: What do you want to feel first thing in the morning? Write it down.
cells.J11: Describe your ideal morning in one page. Which part could you start this week?
cells.C12: Use one device for one task at a time. Close the other tabs and let your attention rest in one place.
cells.D12:
Our goal isn’t abstinence; it’s consciousness.

Catherine Price, How to Break Up with Your Phone
cells.E12: Watch one video with full attention, no tab-switching.
cells.F12: Work for one focused hour, phone in another room and one tab open, and notice how your mind settles.
cells.G12: Write one message from start to finish without opening another app.
cells.H12: For a week, use a focus app or timer to block other apps during your main task.
cells.I12: When did you last do just one thing at a time? Write a few lines about how it went.
cells.J12: For 5 days, jot down one task you did single-mindedly and how it compared to multitasking.
cells.C13: Check email, social media and messages only at set times, for example twice a day.
cells.D13:
In a world of distraction, focusing is a superpower.

Ryan Holiday, Discipline Is Destiny
cells.E13: Check messages only after lunch and after dinner today, and notice the quiet in between.
cells.F13: Set two tech windows a day for a week and notice how your focus shifts.
cells.G13: Write your two check-in times on a sticky note and put it on your screen.
cells.H13: For a week, group your online chores (banking, shopping, bills) into one weekly session.
cells.I13: Which messages truly need a fast reply? Write down the few that do.
cells.J13: After a week of batching, journal: what did you gain, and what, if anything, did you miss?
cells.C14: Commit to at least one meal a day completely free of digital devices.
cells.D14:
Checking your phone is like picking your nose: there’s nothing wrong with it, but no one should have to watch you do it.

Catherine Price, How to Break Up with Your Phone
cells.E14: Eat one meal today with your phone out of sight. Savor the first three bites.
cells.F14: Make a tech-free dinner your daily ritual for a week, even when eating alone. Light a candle.
cells.G14: Put a small basket by the table where phones rest during meals.
cells.H14: Invite others to a screen-free lunch and talk about how it feels.
cells.I14: What do you miss when you eat with a screen? Write one sentence.
cells.J14: Write three rules for mindful meals and try them for a week.
cells.C15: Go somewhere today without your phone: a walk, a café, an errand. Notice how you feel.
cells.D15:
Simply put, humans are not wired to be constantly wired.

Cal Newport, Digital Minimalism
cells.E15: Walk to the corner store without your phone and notice the sounds around you.
cells.F15: Spend two hours outdoors without any digital devices.
cells.G15: Go to a café with a book or journal instead of your phone.
cells.H15: Take a weekend hike without GPS, using a printed map.
cells.I15: How did you feel without your phone: anxious, free, or both? Write it down.
cells.J15: Write a page that begins: ‘When I'm away from my phone, I discover…’
cells.C16: Turn off all screens 1 to 2 hours before bed. Use this time to stretch, read, or prepare for the next day.
cells.D16:
We wake up before our devices do, and they ‘go to bed’ before we do.

Andy Crouch, The Tech-Wise Family
cells.E16: Switch off all screens an hour before bed and notice how your eyes and mind feel as you read a paper book.
cells.F16: Build a calming 90-minute pre-bed routine with music, stretching and journaling, and keep it for a week.
cells.G16: Set a screen cutoff alarm and put your devices in another room.
cells.H16: For a week, use your screen-free hour to lay out tomorrow's clothes and plan your day on paper.
cells.I16: What do you usually reach for a screen for at night? Write down what else could meet that need.
cells.J16: For 2 weeks, keep a sleep journal comparing nights with and without screens.
cells.C17: Try a half-day digital sabbath. No screens unless essential: immerse yourself in real life.
cells.D17:
A day without the sensory food of e-mail, videos, books, and conversations is a chance to clear our mind.

Thich Nhat Hanh, Silence
cells.E17: Put away screens for a Saturday morning and take a mindful walk.
cells.F17: From Friday dinner to Saturday lunch, unplug and notice what you miss and what you gain.
cells.G17: Set out analog fun (books, puzzles, cards) and invite your family to join.
cells.H17: Host a phone-free picnic or board game gathering.
cells.I17: Read a little about Shabbat. What could a weekly day of rest bring to your life?
cells.J17: Write your own ritual plan: what you'll do during a half-day tech break.
cells.C18: Find creative replacements: swap Instagram for sketching, news apps for journaling, TikTok for tea and a book.
cells.D18:
There is nourishment in pursuits that have no purpose—that is their purpose.

Ryan Holiday, Stillness Is the Key
cells.E18: Next time you reach to scroll, doodle for 5 minutes instead. Notice how your hand and mind feel.
cells.F18: For a week, replace evening scrolling with journaling, sketching or watercolor.
cells.G18: Take a 20-minute photo walk with a real camera, or your phone in airplane mode.
cells.H18: Sign up for an offline creative class: pottery, improv or painting.
cells.I18: What did you love making as a child? Write down one thing you could try again.
cells.J18: For a week, journal about how making things by hand changes your sense of time.
cells.C19: Try analog tools for tasks you usually do on a screen. Rediscover the joy of a paper notebook.
cells.D19:
The heart of our home is built around things older and better than the newest thing.

Andy Crouch, The Tech-Wise Family
cells.E19: Use a paper to-do list today instead of an app, and enjoy crossing things off.
cells.F19: Switch your calendar, journal and notes to paper for a week, and notice how it feels.
cells.G19: Buy a small notebook and carry it for notes, ideas and reminders.
cells.H19: For two weeks, swap one screen habit for an analog one: a wristwatch, a paper map or a cookbook.
cells.I19: Which task feels better on paper than on a screen? Write down why.
cells.J19: After a week, make a pros and cons list of the paper tools you've tried.
cells.C20: Make a call instead of texting. Meet someone in person. Let human connection replace screen time today.
cells.D20:
The socializing that counts is real conversation, and text is no longer a sufficient alternative.

Cal Newport, Digital Minimalism
cells.E20: Call a friend instead of texting, and listen closely to their voice.
cells.F20: Meet someone for a screen-free coffee and share how you're both feeling.
cells.G20: Greet a neighbor or coworker face-to-face today.
cells.H20: For a week, replace one text conversation a day with a call or a visit.
cells.I20: Who do you text most but rarely see? Write down one way to meet them.
cells.J20: For a week, journal about your in-person moments: which ones left you feeling most alive?
cells.C21: Notice when you reach for your phone out of boredom. Sit with the urge for a few minutes and see if it passes.
cells.D21:
In Zen they say: If something is boring after two minutes, try it for four... Eventually one discovers that it is not boring at all.

J. Cage in Jenny Odell, How to Do Nothing
cells.E21: Sit on a bench for 10 minutes without reaching for anything. Just notice.
cells.F21: Once a day for a week, wait in line without your phone and feel the urge rise and fall.
cells.G21: Next time you feel bored, do one small chore by hand instead of picking up your phone.
cells.H21: Spend a day without headphones and do ordinary tasks with full presence.
cells.I21: What are you avoiding when you reach for your phone out of boredom? Write it down.
cells.J21: For a week, keep a notebook nearby and jot down the ideas that come when you do nothing.
cells.C22: Try a device-free stretch from Friday evening to Saturday noon. Let this time hold space for real life.
cells.D22:
The world is like muddy water. To see through it, we have to let things settle.

Ryan Holiday, Stillness Is the Key
cells.E22: Spend Friday night device-free: light candles or take a bath instead.
cells.F22: Extend your detox until Saturday noon and notice how your mind shifts.
cells.G22: Put all your devices in a box and enjoy analog fun for one evening.
cells.H22: Take a nature walk, garden or visit a museum, all without devices.
cells.I22: Write down what feels hardest about being offline.
cells.J22: After the detox, write about what you missed and what you didn't, and what that says about your habits.
cells.C23: Write your personal tech manifesto: based on the last 3 weeks, what boundaries and habits will support your values from now on?
cells.D23:
Build a life that you don’t need to escape from.

Ryan Holiday, Stillness Is the Key
cells.E23: Choose 3 words you want your tech use to reflect, such as calm, depth or connection.
cells.F23: Read your 3 words aloud each morning for a week and notice how they guide your choices.
cells.G23: Stick a note near your desk with one intention: ‘I use tech to create, not to escape.’
cells.H23: Write and decorate a personal contract with your digital boundaries and commitments.
cells.I23: Which screen habits fit your life goals, and which don't? Write one of each.
cells.J23: Imagine yourself a year from now with healthy tech habits. Write a letter describing a typical day.
cells.C24: Compare today to day 1. Notice what has shifted over these three weeks, and set your own terms for the slip-ups ahead.
cells.D24:
What unplugging lets us do is reflect on the past, present, and future.

Tiffany Shlain, 24/6
cells.E24: Notice one feeling that's different from day 1, maybe calmer or lighter. Name it.
cells.F24: Each evening this week, take a quiet minute to feel what the detox has given you.
cells.G24: Reread your day 1 notes and jot down what's different now.
cells.H24: Put your day 20 contract where you'll see it daily, and set a monthly check-in.
cells.I24: Name one slip-up you expect ahead, and decide now it won't mean starting over.
cells.J24: Write your restart rule for lapses: no guilt, just the next pickup done differently.
